client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on my chest all day, and I can't stop worrying about my mom because she's taking it really hard and I don't know how to be there for her the right way. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, even through the doubt that it might help — that took courage, and it tells me a part of you is still looking for a way through this. Losing your grandmother while also holding worry for your mom sounds exhausting, like you're carrying grief and caregiving at the same time without much space for your own pain. I'd love to start by asking — when you notice that heaviness on your chest, what does it feel like your heart most needs right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I sit with that question, the first thing that comes up is that I just want someone to tell me it's okay that I'm sad, because most of the time I feel like I should be focusing on my mom instead of my own feelings. I think what I need is permission, somehow, to actually grieve without feeling guilty about it. But then I immediately think, who's going to give my mom that same space if I'm busy feeling sorry for myself?
therapist: What you just said is so important — it *is* okay that you're sad, and grief isn't something you earn by finishing your caregiving duties first. I notice there's a kind of quiet exhaustion in the way you're holding all of this, like you're speaking gently around a very heavy truth. I want to gently challenge that thought that it's either you *or* your mom who gets to grieve — what might it look like if both of you were allowed to hurt at the same time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but I honestly don't know what that would even look like in practice. Like, when I'm around my mom, I automatically go into this mode where I'm checking on her, making sure she's eating, trying to say the right things, and there's no room for me to also be falling apart. I guess I'm scared that if I let myself really grieve around her, it'll make things worse for her, like I'll become another burden she has to carry.
therapist: That fear of becoming a burden makes so much sense, and it sounds like it's been quietly running the show every time you're with her — almost like you've taken on a role that doesn't leave room for you to also be a grieving granddaughter. I'm curious about that word "burden" though — is that something your mom has ever actually communicated to you, or is it more of a story you're telling yourself to protect her? Sometimes the most loving thing we can offer someone isn't our strength, but our honesty that we're hurting too.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: No, my mom has never actually said anything like that, you're right about that. It's more like this assumption I've been carrying around, maybe because she always seemed so strong when I was growing up and I never wanted to be the one who made things harder for her. But even knowing that it might just be a story I'm telling myself, I don't know if I can just switch that off — it's so deeply ingrained that the idea of crying in front of her or saying "I'm struggling too" feels almost physically impossible.
therapist: You just made a really meaningful connection — recognizing that this is a learned assumption, not a fact your mom has ever confirmed, is actually a significant insight. It sounds like you grew up reading her strength as a signal that vulnerability wasn't welcome, and over time that became a rule you internalized so deeply it now feels like truth written into your body. I'm wondering — if your mom were sitting here right now and heard you say "I'm struggling too," what do you imagine her face would actually look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: When I actually try to picture her face, I think she would probably cry, and not in a bad way — more like she'd be relieved that she wasn't alone in it. But then I immediately second-guess that image and wonder if I'm just telling myself what I want to see, because the thought of actually testing it in real life still terrifies me. It's easier to imagine it here than to think about doing it for real.
therapist: That image you just described — your mom crying with relief — feels really significant, and I don't think you should be so quick to dismiss it as wishful thinking, because it came from somewhere deep and honest in you. There's something tender in the way you're holding both that hope and that fear at the same time, like you can almost see the door but aren't ready to walk through it yet. What do you think would need to feel true, or safe enough, for that terrifying step to feel even just a little more possible?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what would help is if I could somehow practice saying it out loud before I actually have to say it to her, because right now even forming the words "I'm struggling too" feels like it gets stuck somewhere in my throat. Maybe if I could get used to the idea of being vulnerable without it feeling like a catastrophe, the real conversation might feel less impossible. But I also worry that if I overthink it and plan it too much, it'll come out sounding rehearsed and then the whole moment will feel fake.
therapist: What you're describing is actually a really healthy instinct — there's a difference between rehearsing words until they feel mechanical and simply giving yourself enough safe exposure to vulnerability that it stops feeling catastrophic. You might not need a script so much as a few small moments of practice, like saying it out loud to yourself, or even here with me, where the stakes feel lower. Would you be willing to try saying it right now, just to see what it feels like to let those words exist in the air?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay... I'm struggling too. I actually said it and my eyes got watery just doing it here, which kind of surprised me because I thought I had a better handle on things than that. I guess I didn't realize how much I needed to hear myself say it out loud, but I'm still not sure that feeling it here with you is the same as being able to feel it in front of her.
therapist: You said it — and the fact that your eyes got watery tells you something really important, that those words carry real weight because they're true, not because you're falling apart. There's something quietly powerful about the way you said it just now, soft and a little tentative, like you were testing whether the ground would hold — and it did. What you felt here isn't separate from what you might feel with her; it's actually the same vulnerability, just with the training wheels still on.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That image of training wheels actually makes sense to me, and I think I needed to hear it framed that way. But I'm sitting here thinking that even if I can do this here, the moment I'm actually in my mom's kitchen watching her look tired and sad, all of this is going to fly out the window and I'll just go back to asking her if she's eaten or if she needs anything. I don't know how to hold onto this feeling long enough to carry it into that room with her.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — there's an energy in it, almost like your mind is racing ahead to that kitchen, already bracing for the moment things go sideways. That protective instinct you described, asking if she's eaten, checking on her needs, it isn't going to disappear, but maybe it doesn't have to — maybe it can coexist with one small, honest moment rather than replacing it entirely. What if the goal wasn't to hold onto this whole conversation, but just to carry in one sentence, even imperfectly, even with a shaky voice?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: One sentence feels more manageable than trying to remember everything we talked about, I'll give you that. I think the sentence would probably be something like "I miss her too, Mom," because that feels true and small enough that I might actually be able to get it out. But I'm already imagining the silence after I say it and not knowing what to do with that silence, which is almost scarier than saying the words in the first place.
therapist: "I miss her too, Mom" — that's not small at all, actually, that's exactly the kind of truth that can crack a moment open in the most beautiful way. And that silence you're afraid of? It might just be the two of you finally standing in the same grief together, and sometimes that silence doesn't need to be filled, it just needs to be survived for a few seconds. What if the silence isn't emptiness, but actually the space where she gets to feel less alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: When you put it that way, the silence being the space where she feels less alone, something in me actually relaxed a little, like I'd been holding my breath without realizing it. I think I've been so focused on filling every quiet moment with something useful that I forgot silence can mean something other than failure. I'm still scared, but maybe a little less scared than I was twenty minutes ago.
therapist: That exhale you just described — that's not a small thing, that's your nervous system starting to trust something new. I love that you named it so precisely, that you'd been equating silence with failure, because that's a belief worth holding onto and examining, not just here but in other parts of your life too. You came in today unsure that talking would change anything, and something has already shifted — how does it feel to notice that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
